Pharmacotherapy remains an indispensable component even when other biological treatments are employed. Although medication is also known to exert its effects by enhancing neuroplasticity, its characteristics differ somewhat from other plasticity-enhancing treatments. Medication provides consistent stimuli that facilitate neural reorganization by maintaining stable neurotransmitter levels. This mechanism allows for a high degree of precision, as the gentle and gradual rewiring process supports the modification of synapses specifically "tagged" for reorganization. However, this subtle nature is often insufficient to disrupt the deeply ingrained pathological circuits in treatment-resistant patients. To understand how pharmacotherapy can complement or support other therapeutic interventions, it is useful to examine its effects through the lens of the DPRH framework.

## Disruption

Acute SSRI administration produces an immediate surge in synaptic serotonin concentration followed by a compensatory decrease in serotonergic tone during the first one to two weeks of treatment. This neurochemical destabilization may constitute a disruption phase. Only after chronic administration does enhanced serotonergic transmission become established in cortical and limbic projection regions.

The initial serotonergic perturbation translates into measurable network-level alteration. Even a single dose of escitalopram in healthy volunteers decreased functional connectivity within the DMN [@vandeVen2013] and produced widespread FC changes across multiple resting-state networks [@Klaassens2015]. These findings indicate that acute serotonergic modulation can rapidly perturb the organization of large-scale brain networks. In patients with major depressive disorder, Dutta et al.[@Dutta2019] demonstrated that acute intravenous citalopram rapidly reconfigured DMN intra-network connectivity, modifying the aberrant inclusion of the amygdala within the DMN that characterizes the depressed state.

These rapid neural changes precede any alteration in subjective mood and may be related to the initial side effects of SSRI treatment. The increased anxiety, agitation, insomnia, and irritability during the first days of treatment affects between 4% and 65% of patients initiating antidepressant therapy [@Sinclair2009]. Similarly, the rapid blockade of rewarding and aversive stimulus processing may explain the emotional blunting reported by a substantial proportion of SSRI-treated patients [@McCabe2010]. Much as the disruption induced by ECT produces temporary cognitive impairments, the perturbation in the early phase of pharmacotherapy may represent a necessary transitional stage for subsequent therapeutic benefit, though it offers little immediate gain for the patient.

## Potentiation

From this stage onward, pharmacotherapy begins to exert pronounced neuroplastic effects. As early as 1995, it was demonstrated that chronic antidepressant administration significantly increased BDNF and TrkB mRNA expression in the rat hippocampus [@Nibuya1995]. This finding gave rise to the neurotrophic model of depression [@Duman1997; @Duman2006].

Early neuroplasticity theories of antidepressant action emphasized neurogenesis as a primary mechanism. Malberg et al. [@Malberg2000] demonstrated that chronic antidepressant treatment significantly increased the birth of new neurons in the dentate gyrus. Causal evidence was seemingly provided by Santarelli et al. [@Santarelli2003], who showed that the ablation of neurogenesis via irradiation abolished the behavioral effects of both fluoxetine and imipramine in mice. However, this interpretation was subsequently challenged by Bessa et al. [@bessa2008], who demonstrated that the effects persisted even when neurogenesis was pharmacologically suppressed using methylazoxymethanol (MAM). This decoupling of neurogenesis from antidepressant efficacy forced a reevaluation of the neurotrophic hypothesis, shifting the focus from cellular proliferation to synaptic plasticity, such as dendritic remodeling and spine density changes, as the primary substrate of therapeutic action.

The resolution of how monoamine-targeting drugs induce this structural plasticity emerged from studies identifying BDNF-TrkB signaling as a convergent pathway [@Castren2010]. Both SSRIs and psychedelics can directly bind to the transmembrane domain of TrkB neurotrophin receptors, stabilizing its dimer configuration and promoting BDNF signaling independent of increased serotonergic tone [@Casarotto2021; @Moliner2023]. This provided a mechanistic bridge between the monoamine and neurotrophic hypotheses, reconciling the acute biochemical actions of antidepressants with their delayed therapeutic effects without requiring *de novo* neurogenesis.

This mechanistic understanding set the stage for the network hypothesis of antidepressant action [@Castren2013], which conceptualizes depression as a disorder of maladaptive circuit wiring rather than a localized neurochemical deficit. While the effect of SSRIs on serotonergic tone is more modest than that of psychedelics, it similarly reopens critical periods of heightened, juvenile-like plasticity [@Vetencourt2008; @Hensch2005]. According to this model, antidepressants do not merely restore baseline function; rather, they reactivate these critical periods, creating a highly permissive state for experience-dependent rewiring.


## aaa

ECT와 psychedelic의 경우 disruption에 대한 nonspecific repair mechanism의 일환으로 plasticity가 enhance되었다고 생각할 수 있지만, 항우울제는 이러한 추론에 부합하지 않는다. 

SSRIs not only enhance BDNF release but also bind to a transmembrane pocket of the TrkB receptor, facilitating its synaptic localization and increasing BDNF responsiveness [@Casarotto2021; @Saarelainen2003]. Similar mechanism is even more pronounced with psychedelics; LSD and psilocin bind to TrkB with approximately 1,000-fold higher affinity than SSRIs, and their ability to induce dendritic spine growth is strictly dependent on this direct binding [@Moliner2023]. Such direct molecular interactions are difficult to conceptualize as mere compensatory responses to network disruption.

Ketamine presents a more complex, hybrid profile. Its rapid induction of BDNF is largely attributed to the "glutamate burst" resulting from the blockade of NMDA receptors on inhibitory interneurons, which can be regarded a triggered mechanism. However, ketamine’s direct binding to TrkB complicates this interpretation. In contrast, the mechanism for ECT remains the clearest example of triggered potentiation: the massive, global desynchronization and subsequent glutamate surge serve as a powerful stimulus for the expression of BDNF and other neurotrophic factors. Psychedelics likely bridge these two mechanisms, utilizing 5-HT2A-mediated depolarization to trigger widespread disruption while simultaneously engaging direct TrkB signaling.

This suggests a very tentative hypothesis: while a rapid surge in BDNF levels may be a consequence of abrupt neural disruption (as seen in ECT), the enhancement of BDNF *responsiveness* via direct TrkB binding may be an independent, intrinsic property of certain medications. The difference between ketamine and memantine may hint at this dual-path model. Although memantine similarly triggers BDNF release via disinhibition, it lacks the robust antidepressant efficacy of ketamine [@He2021; @Gideons2014]. It is possible that the optimal effect requires the convergence of both direct and triggered potentiation.

## Rewiring

SSRIs promote dendritic remodeling and spine density changes. Even short-term fluoxetine treatment (five days) induced a robust increase in pyramidal cell dendritic spine synapse density in the hippocampus [@Hajszan2005], and the degree of dendritic reorganization correlates with mood-elevating effects [@Bessa2009].

These synaptic-level changes translate into local and global connectivity alterations. Longitudinal neuroimaging studies consistently demonstrate that SSRI treatment normalizes the hyperconnectivity within the DMN [@Posner2013]. A large-scale neuroimaging analysis (more than 1,000 depressed patients) confirmed that medicated patients showed reduced DMN functional connectivity relative to unmedicated patients [@Yan2019]. These changes do not represent random rewiring; rather, they reflect the normalization of anomalous resting-state functional network configurations characteristic of the depressed state [@Dichter2015].

The strengthening of prefrontal regulatory control over limbic structures represents perhaps the most significant change during SSRI treatment. Anand et al. [@Anand2005] demonstrated that six weeks of sertraline treatment significantly increased functional connectivity between the anterior cingulate cortex and limbic regions, reversing the corticolimbic disconnection observed in the depressed state. A subsequent study revealed that as corticolimbic connectivity increased with treatment, limbic activation to negative stimuli decreased [@Anand2007]. These findings suggest that medication did not simply attenuate limbic hyperactivation but fundamentally restructured the regulatory relationship between cortical and subcortical centers.

This rewiring process appears to consolidate the cognitive changes observed early in treatment into therapeutically meaningful outcomes. Catherine Harmer and colleagues proposed a cognitive neuropsychological model that accounts for the delayed onset of therapeutic effect [@Harmer2009]. According to this model, SSRIs produce rapid changes in emotional information processing biases within hours to days [@Godlewska2021], and the therapeutic delay reflects the time required for these corrected biases to translate into sustained mood improvement through ongoing social and environmental interactions [@Harmer2017].

This therapeutic delay presents a critical theoretical challenge when juxtaposed with rapid-acting interventions like ketamine. If ketamine can induce profound synaptic potentiation and symptom relief within hours, it suggests that the protracted rewiring characteristic of traditional antidepressants might reflect a mere pharmacological inefficiency. Consequently, the unique benefit of this gradual reconfiguration requires a robust justification.

Castrén’s iPlasticity theory and network hypothesis may give a clue to the merit of this slow reconfiguration [@Castren2013; @umemori2018]. Ketamine and ECT provoke a rapid, massive surge of synaptogenesis which is aptly called "disruption". However, this immediate perturbation occurs largely independent of environmental context, which may explain why the effects of rapid-acting agents are often transient unless actively consolidated.

In contrast, the slow rewiring driven by chronic SSRI administration provides a sustained, permissive state of plasticity. It sustains the opening state of critical periods [@Vetencourt2008], allowing the brain’s circuitry to be progressively sculpted by the patient’s day-to-day engagement with the world. The protracted temporal trajectory acts as a filter, ensuring that the newly formed connections are continuously shaped by, and adapted to, actual real-world experiences and therapeutic interventions. Therefore, rather than being an inefficient process, the slow action of traditional pharmacotherapy orchestrates a more ecologically valid and stable structural integration. ## Homeostasis

Metaplasticity, or "the plasticity of synaptic plasticity," represents a higher-order regulatory mechanism that modulates the magnitude, threshold, and direction of synaptic changes [@Abraham1996; @Abraham2008]. The nervous system is perpetually confronted with the "stability–plasticity dilemma": it must remain plastic enough to incorporate new information while maintaining the stability of existing networks. Metaplasticity serves as a critical homeostatic mechanism that resolves this dilemma by balancing stability and flexibility across diverse timescales.

### The BCM Model and Threshold Dynamics

The Bienenstock-Cooper-Munro (BCM) theory provides a mathematical formalization of metaplasticity through a sliding modification threshold ($\theta_m$) that separates the induction of LTP from LTD [@Bienenstock1982]. Critically, $\theta_m$ is a function of recent postsynaptic activity history. High prior activity elevates $\theta_m$, making LTP more difficult and preventing runaway excitation, while low average activity lowers the threshold to facilitate LTP.

Major depressive disorder may involve pathologically elevated $\theta_m$, resulting in a plasticity deficit [@duman2012]. The massive, synchronized neural discharge during ECT followed by profound post-ictal suppression may acutely lower $\theta_m$ according to BCM dynamics. This shift creates a state where even modest physiological activity—which would otherwise be insufficient—becomes capable of inducing LTP [@Cooper2012].

## Network-Level Metaplasticity

The concept of metaplasticity extends beyond individual synapses to network-level modularity. The central nervous system is organized into a hierarchical modular structure where local clusters are interconnected to form higher-order functional networks [@Bullmore2012]. While lower-level modules typically comprise anatomically adjacent regions, large-scale networks like DMN consist of long-range connections across spatially segregated structures.

At this scale, metaplasticity is reflected in the flexibility of network reconfiguration and the dynamic range of functional connectivity. Recent research highlights that the ability of the brain to transition between different "attractor states" is a hallmark of healthy cognitive function [@Braun2015; @Arnemann2015; @AvenaKoenigsberger2018]. Metaplasticity governs the ease with which these network states can be perturbed and re-organized [@Scott2023]. Ultimately, metaplasticity should be understood not merely as a molecular phenomenon at the synapse, but as a multi-scale principle defining how the brain maintains and regulates its learnable state [@MllerDahlhaus2015; @Wen2024].

## Homeostatic Plasticity and Resilience

Homeostatic plasticity (HP) is one of the mechanisms of metaplasticity, referring to the capacity of neurons and neural circuits to regulate their own excitability and synaptic strength relative to the overall activity of the network to maintain stability, thereby influencing the future potential for Hebbian forms of plasticity [@Li2019a]. This conceptualization of HP resonates with the definition of resilience proposed by Scheffer et al. [@schefferEtAl2024a] within the dynamical systems framework. Dynamical resilience is defined as the capacity of a system to absorb perturbations without transitioning into alternative pathological attractors. In Scheffer's model, the healthy mental state possesses a basin of attraction whose depth reflects resilience. In a resilient basin, the system can easily return to equilibrium despite transient disturbances. As this basin loses resilience, the risk increases that minor stressors can precipitate a transition into disordered states.

Homeostatic plasticity encompasses a suite of compensatory mechanisms, including synaptic scaling, intrinsic excitability adjustments, and metaplastic modulation of synaptic weights [@Turrigiano2004; @LeRoux2006; @Turrigiano2008; @Siddoway2014]. These implement feedback control loops that counteract deviations from set-point activity levels. When a neural circuit experiences sustained increases in excitatory drive, homeostatic downscaling of excitatory synapses and/or upregulation of inhibitory transmission restores balance. Conversely, prolonged suppression of activity triggers compensatory strengthening of excitatory connections or reduction of inhibitory drive [@Turrigiano1998].

The metaphorical equivalence becomes apparent when considering that HP provides the feedback mechanisms necessary to maintain the basin of attraction. Just as dynamical resilience reflects the capacity to return to baseline, HP represents the neurobiological machinery that ensures a return to the functional set-point. Extending the concept to the psychological domain, high resilience implies the ability to withstand stressors and rapidly return to mental equilibrium.

## Empirical Evidence

Empirical evidence suggests that HP at the circuit level mediates stress resilience at the behavioral level. Research on mesolimbic dopamine circuits has shown that homeostatic adaptations following chronic social defeat stress distinguish resilient from susceptible animals [@Krishnan2007; @Isingrini2016]. Specifically, animals exhibiting behavioral resilience demonstrate compensatory synaptic adjustments in ventral tegmental area dopamine neurons that normalize circuit excitability despite ongoing stress exposure [@Friedman2014]. BDNF is also implicated in HP mechanisms. Animals with enhanced BDNF signaling exhibit greater capacity for homeostatic synaptic adjustments and correspondingly greater behavioral resilience to chronic stress [@Taliaz2011; @Leschik2022].

The concept of "homeostatic disruption or failure" is relevant in understanding depression ([@Naisberg1996]; [@Wang2025];[@Andreescu2019] ). Prolonged or severe perturbations can exhaust homeostatic mechanisms, leading to paradoxical or maladaptive compensatory responses [@Gou2025]. For instance, chronic stress can lead to excessive upregulation of inhibitory transmission in reward circuits, potentially contributing to anhedonia and motivational deficits. What began as a homeostatic response becomes pathological, contributing to the formation of a stable depressive attractor. This aligns with the dynamical systems concept of increasing "bad resilience"—the pathological state becomes increasingly resistant to interventions as maladaptive homeostatic adjustments entrench the disordered circuit configuration [@Christoffel2011; @Bath2017; @Pignatelli2021].

Building on this, Wang et al.[@wang2025] detailed how specific molecular deficits contribute to this homeostatic failure in depression. Altered expression of ion channels compromises intrinsic excitability, preventing neurons from maintaining a stable excitatory-inhibitory (E/I) set point. Furthermore, abnormalities in presynaptic neurotransmitter release, often influenced by glial signals such as TNF-α, impair the homeostatic regulation of network activity. These issues are compounded by deficits in synaptic scaling and signaling molecules, including retinoic acid pathways that modulate postsynaptic AMPA receptor density, which further undermine synaptic stability and entrench the pathological state [@arendt2015;@hu2020].

## Clinical implication of Homeostatic Plasticity

Even if the brain's attractor landscape is restored to a healthy state, maintaining this fragile state necessitates robust HP regulation. HP has essential role in maintaining network stability [@Fernandes2016; @Wu2020]. If HP remains compromised, minor perturbations, such as acute stressors, sleep deprivation, or circadian misalignment, can readily precipitate a transition back into a pathological state. Therefore, the final stage of the DPRH sequence must involve the reinforcement of HP to stabilize the healthy attractor and enhance long-term resilience [@Workman2018].

rTMS, particularly theta burst stimulation (TBS) protocols, has been shown to induce metaplastic effects consistent with homeostatic regulation [@Jones2016; @Tse2018]. Depending on whether the protocol is continuous or intermittent, TBS can induce either LTD or LTP. Furthermore, the magnitude of these effects is modulated by the prior history of circuit activity [@Kirkovski2023]. In individuals with depression, prefrontal circuits often exhibit abnormal metaplasticity characterized by blunted responses to plasticity-inducing protocols [@Cantone2017]. If repeated stimulation sessions were to normalize this metaplastic deficit, it would significantly reduce the risk of relapse by enhancing resilience against future perturbations [@Kavalali2020].

Several pharmacological agents show evidence of promoting homeostatic plasticity. Lithium has been shown to promote homeostatic downscaling of excitatory synaptic strength through effects on glycogen synthase kinase-3β (GSK-3β) signaling. This homeostatic adjustment may stabilize circuits prone to excessive excitability, thereby deepening the basin of attraction around euthymic states [@Salinas1999; @Gideons2017; @MachadoVieira2018; @Kavalali2020]. Valproate modulates GABAergic inhibition and can affect activity-dependent homeostatic plasticity in preclinical models [@Wang2012; @Zhang2003]. Its efficacy in preventing both manic and depressive episodes may reflect stabilization of circuits prone to excessive excitability or hypoactivity through enhanced homeostatic regulation.

Novel compounds targeting metaplastic mechanisms may offer more direct approaches to enhancing homeostatic plasticity. For example, drugs modulating metabotropic glutamate receptors (particularly mGluR2/3 and mGluR5) can shift the threshold for synaptic plasticity induction and affect homeostatic scaling mechanisms [@Hu2010; @Lscher2010]. Similarly, agents affecting neurosteroid synthesis—which modulate GABAA receptor function and have rapid antidepressant effects—may act partly by restoring E-I balance through homeostatic mechanisms [@Diviccaro2022; @Cutler2023].
